name: Dana Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. So you can tell me the public version and the private one. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at six, dogs fed, then out on the quad bike to check the ewes on the hill. We've got about 1,100 on 800 hectares of rough grazing, and it's me, the owner Mr Price, and a part-time lad at lambing. Today was moving a group down off the top ground before the weather turns, with Moss and Fly, my two dogs. I'm still learning, honestly. Mr Price can read a hillside like a newspaper and I'm still at the picture-book stage.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned learning. How do you go about that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Half from Mr Price and half from my phone. I use an AI app every day: I log lambing on it, I photograph a lame ewe's foot and ask what it might be, I ask it to explain the vet's letter in plain words. Mr Price thinks it's witchcraft, but he's started asking me to check things for him. Money-wise, I share a rented house in the village with my friend Kezia and I've got maybe two weeks of savings, so I'm not exactly secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. That would be a bit disappointing, honestly. I quite like my witchcraft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still useful, people just expected magic. I'd tell the other young shepherds at the market to keep using it for the boring stuff, the records and the forms. Online I'd probably post a little thread about the tools that actually help on a hill farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit relieved, because my job's safe. But my job being safe isn't the same as my job being good. I'm on low pay, the house isn't mine, and sheep farming on the hills only works because of public payments. A flop doesn't change who owns the land or how little wool's worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, keep using the app, and try to talk Mr Price into putting GPS collars on a trial group so we don't spend whole days on the quad. I'd start a small side thing, maybe selling sheepskin rugs online, because I'm good with the phone side. And I'd keep pushing for the young farmers' group to talk about pay, not just quiz nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Restless, maybe. Like the weather staying grey for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the collars. What would they do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're called virtual fencing. The sheep wear a collar and it beeps when they get near a line you've drawn on a map, so you don't need a wall or a fence. It would save us rebuilding walls that are older than my great-gran. I've watched about forty videos on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned public payments. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grateful and a bit embarrassed, to be honest. People in town think farmers are rolling in subsidies, and Mr Price drives a fifteen-year-old pickup. I think the payments should be bigger and tied to looking after the land, and that's a fight I'd happily pick.

S0.say: I'd say AI is still useful and people just expected magic. I'd tell other young shepherds to keep using it for records and forms, and post a thread about the tools that help on a hill farm.
S0.think: My job being safe isn't the same as my job being good. A flop doesn't change who owns the land, how little wool is worth or how much hill farming depends on public payments.
S0.do: Keeps using the AI app daily and pushes her boss to trial GPS collars on a group of sheep. Starts selling sheepskin rugs online as a side income and raises pay at the young farmers' group.
S0.feel: Calm but restless, like a grey week of weather.
S0.quote: My job being safe isn't the same as my job being good.
S0.fieldNote: Dana is the most comfortable with AI of anyone so far: she uses it daily and has taught her sceptical boss to rely on it. Her politics are about land ownership and public payments, not technology. Even in a flat picture she is looking for new tools and a side income, which fits her restless, early-mover nature.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh, this is the one I'm actually ready for. Or I like to think I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms like ours should own the robots together, not rent them from some company abroad. I'd say it at the young farmers' group and to anyone at the auction mart who'll listen. Online I'd post about co-ops, because nobody my age can afford a robot on their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do fine in this one, at least for a while. The hill is the last place the robots will manage, with the bogs and the scree and the weather. And I'd be the one who already knows the collars and the drones, so I'd be useful. What worries me is the lad at lambing and the older shepherds who won't touch a phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd get a drone licence, which is about £200 and a weekend course, so I can check the top ground from the yard. I'd set up the collar trial and log everything so we can show the bank and the government it works. Then I'd offer to do the same for two or three neighbouring farms, for a fee, as a side business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. With a little guilt underneath, because I know not everyone's going to feel like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be worried about, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gethin, the lad who helps at lambing. He's 19, he's brilliant with ewes and terrible at reading. If the work turns into screens, he's out, and he's the best natural stockman I've ever met. I'd want to teach him, but I'm not sure he'd want me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the £200 for the drone licence come from, on two weeks of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good question. The rug money, if it's started, or I'd ask Mr Price to pay half since it saves him the diesel. Otherwise I'd skip Christmas presents and tell my family it's an investment. My mum would roll her eyes.

S1.say: I'd say farms like ours should own the robots together through co-ops, not rent them from a company abroad. I'd say it at the young farmers' group, at the auction mart and online.
S1.think: I think I'd do fine for a while, because the hill is the last place robots will manage and I already know the collars and drones. I'm more worried about the young lambing helper and the older shepherds who won't touch a phone.
S1.do: Gets a drone licence for about £200 and runs a logged collar trial to show the bank and government it works. Offers the same service to two or three neighbouring farms for a fee.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with a little guilt because not everyone will feel that way.
S1.quote: He's the best natural stockman I've ever met. I'd want to teach him, but I'm not sure he'd want me to.
S1.fieldNote: Steady Disruption is the picture Dana feels made for, and she moves first and spends money she barely has. Her political answer is co-op ownership of machines. The most striking part was her worry for a 19-year-old helper who is great with animals and weak with reading, which shows she sees who loses even when she wins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, so the hill isn't the last place. The hill's just another place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why the machines have to be publicly owned or co-op owned, because otherwise a few companies own all the work. I'd be shouting it at the young farmers and the local council. Online I'd be calmer than people expect, sharing practical stuff: what support exists, who to call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, two years is scary even for me. I'm good at learning new tools, but if the tool can do the whole job, being good with the tool doesn't help for long. My bet is I'd get maybe a year running the robots on our hill before they don't need me either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. In the first month I'd go to Mr Price and say let me set up the robots and the drones, don't buy a company to do it. I'd learn everything about how they're run, and start offering it to other hill farms. If that dried up after a year, I'd move to wherever the jobs were being invented, probably a city, even though I'd hate leaving the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Fired up, but anxious. Like going down a steep track on the quad, knowing you can't brake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would leaving the hill mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would break my heart a bit. I grew up in a town and chose this, I wasn't born to it. So leaving would feel like failing at the one thing I picked for myself. Moss and Fly wouldn't do well in a flat, either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years with two weeks of savings. How would that work in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It wouldn't, not without help. I'd need the rug business and the robot work to pay something quickly. And I'd lean on Kezia, splitting things, and on whatever support the government puts out. I'm not proud, I'd take it.

S2.say: I'd say this is why the machines have to be publicly owned or owned by co-ops, otherwise a few companies own all the work. Online I'd share practical help, like what support exists and who to call.
S2.think: Even for me, two years is scary. If the tool can do the whole job, being good with the tool only helps for about a year before the robots don't need me either.
S2.do: Asks her boss in the first month to let her set up the robots and drones herself, then offers that service to other hill farms. If that work dries up within a year, moves to a city where new jobs are being created.
S2.feel: Anxious and fired up, like going down a steep track on the quad without brakes.
S2.quote: If the tool can do the whole job, being good with the tool doesn't help for long.
S2.fieldNote: Dana's confidence holds better than most, but she sees that her edge, being early with tools, wears off fast if the tools do everything. Her plan is to move first and then move away if needed. The hard part is emotional: she chose this life, so leaving would feel like failing at the thing she picked for herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is more my speed. I could actually build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to set up farm co-ops that own the machines and share the profits, and we should start now. I'd ask the council and the farming union for help. Online I'd be the one posting how-to videos, because I'm going to be doing it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is the sweet spot for someone like me: long enough to build a little business, short enough that most people won't have started. The risk is I build a business that lasts three years and then gets swallowed. But three good years would be more than I've had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd do the drone licence and a course in robotics maintenance, probably online in the evenings. By year two I'd have a small business running drones and collars for six or seven hill farms. And I'd put every spare pound into a savings account, because I'd want at least three months' cushion before it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than not. I like having a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that a contradiction, saying machines should be shared while you build your own business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, maybe. I'd want it to be a co-op, with the farms owning a share. I'm not trying to be a tech boss. But yes, if nobody else moved, I'd start it myself and fix the ownership later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Gethin in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say come work with me. You know the sheep, I know the machines, and for five years that's a better team than either of us alone. I'd pay him properly too, once there's money.

S3.say: We've got five years to set up farm co-ops that own the machines and share the profits, so let's start now. I'd ask the council and the farming union for help and post how-to videos online.
S3.think: Five years is the sweet spot for someone like me: long enough to build something, short enough that most people won't have started. Even if the business only lasts three years, that's more than I've had.
S3.do: Gets a drone licence and studies robotics maintenance online in year one. By year two runs a drone and collar service for six or seven hill farms and saves every spare pound to reach three months' cushion.
S3.feel: Uneasy but more hopeful than not, glad of a head start.
S3.quote: If nobody else moved, I'd start it myself and fix the ownership later.
S3.fieldNote: The five-year picture is where Dana's progressive views and her adaptability pull against each other, and she admitted it with a laugh. She would prefer a co-op but would start alone if no one else moved. Her plan for Gethin, pairing animal skill with machine skill, came naturally and suggests she thinks in teams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to do something properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to plan, so there's no excuse for not doing it fairly. I'd push for a law that shares the gains, maybe a basic income, because everyone's going to need it eventually. Online I'd share the hopeful stuff, the projects that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years makes me think bigger. I could maybe get a share in a farm, or set up a co-op properly. But I'd be 37, and if all the work goes, I'd want to have done something worth doing with those ten years, not just kept busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first two years I'd do the drone and robotics training and the collar business, like the other pictures. Then I'd go to college part-time for land management, because when the robots do the sheep, someone still has to decide what the hills are for. By year five I'd want to be in a co-op that owns its own machines and some land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit hopeful. Ten years feels like a career, not a countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean, someone has to decide what the hills are for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether it's sheep, trees, peat bogs or walkers. The robots can do the work, but someone has to choose, and I'd want it to be people who live here. That's the bit I'd fight for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you leave farming altogether in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the land all gets bought up by people who never come here. Then there'd be nothing to stay for. But with ten years, I'd at least have a chance to stop that.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time to plan, so there's no excuse for not doing it fairly. I'd push for a law that shares the gains, maybe a basic income, and share the hopeful projects online.
S4.think: Ten years makes me think bigger, like a share in a farm or a proper co-op. But I'd be 37, and if all the work goes, I'd want to have done something worth doing, not just kept busy.
S4.do: Builds the drone and collar business in the first two years, then studies land management part-time. Aims to be in a co-op that owns its own machines and some land by year five.
S4.feel: Calm and a bit hopeful; ten years feels like a career, not a countdown.
S4.quote: The robots can do the work, but someone has to choose, and I'd want it to be people who live here.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Dana's focus shifts from keeping a job to deciding what the land is for, which is a striking leap. She sees a future role in choices, not labour. Her one fear is absentee buyers taking the land, which ties back to her first answer about who owns it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because I couldn't learn fast enough, but because there's no time to build anything before it's gone, and I've got nothing saved to fall back on. What would help is cheap loans or grants for small co-ops to buy their own machines, and some sort of basic income, so people like Gethin aren't left with nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the land. Everyone asks who owns the robots, but on the hill it's the land that matters. If big buyers own the land and the machines, then it doesn't matter how adaptable I am.

headlineQuote: If the tool can do the whole job, being good with the tool doesn't help for long.
portrait: Dana Chen is a 27-year-old junior shepherd on a hill farm with about 1,100 ewes, who works with her two dogs and an AI app she uses every day. She grew up in a town and chose farming, shares a rented house with a friend and has about two weeks of savings. She is the first to try new tools and sees the Steady Disruption picture as her chance, but in AGI by 2028 she knows her head start wears off fast. Given five or ten years, she plans a drone and collar service and then a co-op that owns machines and land. Her politics centre on ownership: who owns the robots, and above all who owns the hills.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be no time to build anything and no savings to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans or grants for small co-ops to buy their own machines, and a basic income so people like her lambing helper aren't left with nothing.
